The test image shows a split soybean stem with:
- Large black sclerotia (hard, black bodies) inside the stem cavity
- White fluffy mycelial growth on the stem
- Bleached/whitened stem tissue
- This is clearly a stem-affected specimen

This strongly suggests **White Mold**. Now I'll check the part index and then view reference images from 8 different classes.

The test image is a stem. Stem candidates: Anthracnose, Brown_Stem_Rot, Charcoal_Rot, Diaporthe, Fusarium, Green_stem_disorder, Phytophthora, Pythium_damping_off, Rhizoctonia, Tobacco_Streak_Virus, White_Mold.

The large black sclerotia + white mycelium strongly point to White_Mold. Let me verify with reference images across 8 classes.
White_Mold reference shows black sclerotia on stems - matches. Now checking other candidates.
Charcoal_Rot shows fine gray mottling, not the large discrete black sclerotia. Let me check more classes.
Brown_Stem_Rot shows brown pith discoloration, no sclerotia. Continuing with more classes.
This White_Mold reference shows the elongated black sclerotium on stem surface + fluffy white mycelium - very close match to the test image. Let me view one more class.

All evidence is clear. Summary of findings:

- **Test image**: Split soybean stem showing large black sclerotia inside the cavity + white fluffy mycelium + bleached stem tissue
- **White_Mold refs** (views 1 & 8): Both show characteristic black sclerotia and white mycelium - direct match
- **Charcoal_Rot**: Tiny scattered microsclerotia giving gray appearance - different scale/pattern
- **Anthracnose**: Small black acervuli on stem surface - no large sclerotia
- **Brown_Stem_Rot**: Brown pith discoloration, no black bodies
- **Phytophthora**: Chocolate-brown stem, no sclerotia
- **Rhizoctonia**: Reddish-brown sunken canker at soil line
- **Fusarium**: Brown vascular tissue, no sclerotia
- **Tobacco_Streak_Virus**: Node discoloration only

The large black sclerotia embedded inside the bleached stem with white mycelium is the pathognomonic sign of White_Mold (Sclerotinia stem rot). No other stem disease produces these large, hard, black bodies inside the stem cavity.
